title: Nanometer Design Studies
intro: This chapter puts the earlier ones to work: two complete op-amp designs in a 40 nm process with a 1 V supply, carried out the way a designer actually works, with simulated device curves, quick feasibility estimates, bias and common-mode loops, compensation and power scaling (Razavi, Chapter 11).

blocks.text: What changes in a nanometer process

Short devices do not follow the square law: velocity saturation and mobility degradation bend the $I_D$-$V_{DS}$ and $g_m$ curves, channel-length modulation is so strong that triode and saturation barely separate, and a 1 V supply leaves a few hundred millivolts of headroom per device. The small-signal model still holds; only the relations between $g_m$, $r_O$ and bias change. So sizing is done from simulated curves of one reference transistor, scaled to the required current.

Typical 40 nm numbers used here: intrinsic gain $g_mr_O$ of about 7 to 10 for NMOS and 5 to 7 for PMOS at minimum length; a knee (saturation onset) below $V_{DS} = 0.2$ V even at 350 mV of overdrive; and $\xi \approx 1.5$ in weak inversion so $g_m \le I_D/(1.5V_T)$.

items: Designing with Modern Transistors: velocity saturation, mobility degradation, ways to scale $g_m$, and sizing from a reference transistor for given $I_D$, $V_{DS,min}$ and $g_m$.
Telescopic Op Amp Design: why a single cascode stage cannot reach a gain of 500 at 1 V, bias circuits, common-mode feedback with complementary followers, and CM loop stability.
Two-Stage Op Amp Design: splitting power, choosing the output device, simple resistive CMFB, Miller compensation with a zero-moving resistor, and closed-loop checks.
High-Speed Amplifier Design: a gain-of-4 capacitive-feedback amplifier settling in 5 ns, compensation for $\beta < 1$, linear power scaling and large-signal fixes.

blocks.text: The method in one line: understand the root cause of each problem, change only the parameter tied to it, and check everything in closed loop at the end, including corners, temperature and supply.

blocks.title: A quick feasibility check
blocks.text: A single-stage cascode amplifier in this process needs a gain of 500. With $g_mr_O \approx 8$ for every device, what is the best gain a cascode with cascode load can give? Is a single stage feasible?
solution: A cascode stage gives roughly $(g_mr_O)^2/2$ when the NMOS and PMOS cascodes have similar output resistance: $64/2 = 32$, and at best $(g_mr_O)^2 = 64$ if the load were ideal.
Both are far below 500, so two stages are needed.
blocks.answer: About 30 to 60: not feasible in one stage.
